title: Salesforce FIDE World Championship Match 2026: Schedule, format, and prize fund confirmed
summary: FIDE is pleased to announce the regulations for the Salesforce FIDE World Championship Match 2026, confirming the venue, format, schedule, and prize distribution for the meeting between reigning World Champion Grandmaster Gukesh D and his challenger, Grandmaster Javokhir Sindarov. The match will be held at the Fondation Martin Bodmer in Cologny, Geneva, Switzerland, from 22 November to 12 December 2026, bringing a World Championship match back to Switzerland for the first time since Brissago in 2004. The official programme opens on 22 November with Media Day and the Opening Ceremony. The first classical game will be played on 24 November, and the final scheduled game on 11 December. Tiebreaks, if required, will follow on 12 December. Gukesh and Sindarov will both be 20 when the match begins, making this the youngest World Championship contest in history. For Gukesh, Geneva will mark the first defence of the title he won in Singapore in 2024. Sindarov arrives as the winner of both the 2025 FIDE World Cup and the 2026 FIDE Candidates Tournament. “A World Championship match is not like anything else in our sport,” said Viswanathan Anand, FIDE Interim President. “You sit across from the same opponent for three weeks with the world watching. I have played World Championship matches in some extraordinary cultural settings, including the Olympic Museum in Lausanne and the Bundeskunsthalle in Bonn, and a setting like that gives the contest a character of its own. The Fondation Martin Bodmer belongs to that tradition and is a fitting venue for this match.” The players Gukesh D, representing India, became the 18th World Champion in December 2024. He defeated Ding Liren 7.5-6.5 after winning the fourteenth and final classical game in Singapore. At 18, he became the youngest undisputed World Champion in chess history. His road to the title also included victory at the 2024 FIDE Candidates Tournament and individual and team gold medals at the 2024 Chess Olympiad. Javokhir Sindarov, representing Uzbekistan, qualified for the match by winning the 2026 FIDE Candidates Tournament in Cyprus. He secured first place with a round to spare, finished unbeaten and scored 10/14. That result came less than five months after he became the youngest winner of the FIDE World Cup in Goa. Sindarov is the first player from Uzbekistan to qualify for a match for the undisputed World Championship title. Match format The match consists of a maximum of 14 classical games. The first player to reach 7.5 points wins the match and the title. The time control is 120 minutes for the first 40 moves, followed by 30 minutes for the rest of the game. A 30-second increment is added from move 41. Draw offers are not permitted before Black’s 40th move. Before that point, a draw may be claimed through the Chief Arbiter or Deputy Chief Arbiter only in cases of threefold repetition or stalemate. If the score is 7-7 after the classical games, the title will be decided on 12 December. The tiebreak begins with four games at 15 minutes plus a 10-second increment per move. If the score remains level, the players contest two games at 10 minutes plus five seconds, followed, if necessary, by two games at three minutes plus two seconds. Should the tie persist, three-minute-plus-two-second games will be played one at a time, with colours reversed after each draw, until a decisive result is reached. USD 2.5 million prize fund The prize fund is USD 2.5 million, net of any applicable local taxes. Under the standard distribution, each player receives USD 200,000 for every game won, including a win by forfeit, and the remaining balance is divided equally between the two players. If the final classical score is 7.5-6.5 with 13 decisive games, or 8-6 with all 14 games decisive, the winner will receive USD 1.3 million and the runner-up USD 1.2 million. The same USD 1.3 million to USD 1.2 million split applies if the match is decided in tiebreaks. Sponsor Salesforce joined FIDE as Title Sponsor and Technological Partner in September 2026. The multi-year agreement covers the World Championship Matches in 2026 and 2028 as well as the Women’s World Championship Match in 2027. Salesforce is also the official AI partner of the FIDE World Chess Championship and the FIDE rankings, and the agreement brings its Agentforce 360 portfolio, including Slack, to FIDE events and to the rating list.  The venue  Founded in 1971, the Fondation Martin Bodmer is a heritage library and museum that houses and exhibits the greatest texts of world literature and human history. This unique place presents major testimonies of human thought from the origins of writing to the present day. The Fondation holds some 150,000 documents in nearly 120 languages, making up one of the finest private collections in the world. It includes hundreds of papyri, Western and Eastern medieval manuscripts, and thousands of pages of autograph manuscripts and rare engravings. This Bibliotheca Bodmeriana has been inscribed, since 2015, on UNESCO’s “Memory of the World” register, an initiative aimed at preserving and disseminating the world’s documentary heritage. The Fondation Martin Bodmer carries out a range of conservation, restoration and digitisation projects with a view to making its documents available online. Since 2003, it has welcomed visitors to its modern underground museum designed by the great Swiss architect Mario Botta, in the incomparable setting of the Cologny hillside where it stands, with breathtaking views over Lake Geneva and the city of Geneva. In addition to its permanent exhibition, the Fondation Martin Bodmer organises temporary exhibitions and cultural outreach activities on themes related to science, the arts, history and literature, giving the public access to these authentic treasures that have shaped the history of humanity. Bringing the World Championship to the Fondation places one of the greatest contests of chess within a venue devoted to preserving the history of ideas. “We are thrilled and delighted to welcome this global event to our institution. title: From inclusion to inspiration: Three teams lead after Day 3 in Samarkand
summary: Day 3 of the 3rd FIDE Chess Olympiad for People with Disabilities began with a panel discussion on inclusion and technology in chess before attention returned to the boards, where the race at the top narrowed to just three teams with perfect scores. The morning discussion brought together players, coaches, officials and federation representatives and followed a presentation by a professor, Dr. Kubanych Takyrbashev, from the American University of Technology in Tashkent. Participants exchanged ideas on how technology can improve accessibility, as well as on education, training, chess in schools and creating more opportunities for players with disabilities. For GM Thomas Luther, Chairperson of the FIDE Commission for Players with Disabilities, technological development can help reduce barriers. “People with disabilities have disadvantages, but technology actually can be an equalizer. With technology, we already see that people can work on computers and phones and have all sorts of different gadgets to make their lives better. But now with AI, things come to a new level.” Luther also highlighted the significance of holding the Olympiad for People with Disabilities alongside the 46th FIDE Chess Olympiad in Samarkand. “It’s not like one event is singled out; it’s overlapping. We are a family in FIDE. Gens Una Sumus is not just a motto – we are really living it.” For Jamie Kenmure, Chairman of the Asian Commission for People with Disabilities and Chancellor of the FIDE DIS Commission, the discussion also provided an opportunity to listen directly to what federations and players need. “We need more education, more awareness, visibility, empowerment. This is the key message: empowerment.” And for Kenmure, that empowerment is ultimately about the participants themselves. “The people who really make the tournament are the players themselves. They are the ones who should feel special. It’s their moment to shine.” From world champion to coach of champions One of those players competing in Samarkand is FM Sirojiddin Zaynidinov of Uzbekistan, a two-time world champion in deaf chess whose influence on Uzbek chess extends well beyond his own results. Zaynidinov lost his hearing after becoming ill at around the age of three. At five, his father introduced him to chess, beginning a journey that would eventually take him to world titles. Growing up, he was often the only deaf child among hearing players at his chess club. “All the other children in the chess club were hearing, and I was the only deaf child among them. But that never bothered me. I enjoyed playing chess with them.” At the age of 14, Zaynidinov won a World Youth Championship in Germany in 2004. Four years later, he won another world title in Switzerland. But after becoming a champion himself, Zaynidinov decided that his next goal would be to help others achieve the same. “I didn’t want only to be a champion myself – I wanted to teach others and have students who could become champions too.” Among the children who later arrived at his chess club was five-year-old Javokhir Sindarov. Zaynidinov immediately recognised his potential. Communication initially required some adaptation: he used visual explanations and repeated words when necessary, while Sindarov gradually learned to understand his articulation and speech. The young player’s progress was rapid. By eight, Sindarov’s rating was already around 1900. “I was convinced that by the age of 12 he would become a grandmaster. I had that feeling. I was sure of it.” Sindarov later continued working with other coaches, but Zaynidinov had provided the foundation. His student’s success also brought more parents and young players to Zaynidinov’s chess club. The relationship between the two has remained strong. “When he became a champion, he would still come to me and greet me. I am very happy that he has never forgotten that I was his teacher.” Their paths now cross again in Samarkand: Zaynidinov is competing in the Olympiad for People with Disabilities, while Sindarov is preparing to play in the 46th FIDE Chess Olympiad. A first Olympiad for Eswatini’s Mlandvo Khumalo For Mlandvo Khumalo of Team Eswatini, Samarkand represents a different milestone: his first FIDE Chess Olympiad for People with Disabilities. Khumalo discovered chess at secondary school after his teacher, Mr Malaza, encouraged him to try the game. At first, he was unsure whether chess was for him. “The first time he said that I must try it, I thought this was a game for other people, not for someone like me. But he gave me the energy to go and play chess.” Once Khumalo began learning the moves, his perception changed. His school team later finished second in a tournament, strengthening his desire to continue. “That was when I realized that I have to play chess, and that it is a good sport. It opens the mind.” Khumalo lost both hands following a serious illness during infancy. Today, he manages most aspects of everyday life independently: he writes, uses his phone and plays chess, moving the pieces with his arms. In Samarkand, however, the experience has been about more than the games. “I like playing with different teams, getting to know different people and seeing different kinds of people. It makes me feel inside that I am part of the people.” And his description of what happens when a game begins reveals the enthusiasm that brought him this far. “When the opponent pushes the pawn, I feel like we are in a war. I like to defend. It makes me excited, and it opens my mind.” Three teams on 6/6 On the boards, Round 3 significantly narrowed the group at the top of the standings. After eight teams entered the day with perfect scores, only Cuba, Israel and the Czech Republic emerged from the third round on 6/6. The result sets up a direct confrontation between two of the leaders in Round 4, when Cuba face Israel, while the Czech Republic take on Germany. With the tournament moving towards its decisive stages, the leading group is beginning to take shape – but the stories emerging from Samarkand continue

title: Samarkand ready for a record-breaking Chess Olympiad
summary: For centuries, Samarkand stood at the crossroads of civilisations. Merchants, scholars and travellers crossed the ancient Silk Road, carrying ideas and cultures from one part of the world to another. Now, another kind of journey will bring the world to the legendary city: 400 chess teams from across the globe will gather for the 46th FIDE Chess Olympiad. Every two years, national teams from almost every corner of the globe meet across the board, to celebrate the game’s extraordinary international reach.From September 16 (round one) to the 27, Samarkand will feature 208 teams in the Open section and 192 teams in the Women’s event. The figure smashes the previous record of 380 teams set in Budapest in 2024. Players, arbiters, coaches and captains have already started to arrive. Although the bulk of the participants will join the event tomorrow, many of us flew in early this morning on a plane packed with International Grandmasters. On arrival, the special bus decoration immediately caught my attention – the local organisation team have not left anything to chance! Instead of caravans crossing the ancient routes, on this occasion modern transports such as the modern Uzbekistan 210km/hAfrosiyob fast train will connect players, cultures and ideas between East and West. Numbers aside, the Olympiad is unique because it combines the highest level of competitive chess with the opportunity for federations at very different stages of development to share the same stage.And there is definitely no shortage of sporting intrigue! Team India arrive as the defending Open champions after their historic triumph in Budapest, while the United States, China, Germany are among many other established chess powers seeking gold. In a recent interview, India’s captain GM Srinath Narayanan reflected on his team’s chances: “Defending an Olympiad title is always a tough challenge. But this Indian team has a lot going for it. There is continuity in the squad, the players are more experienced. India has brilliant depth across the boards.” Of course, the home team Uzbekistan, surprise winners in 2022, will also carry enormous expectations, having emerged as one of the leading chess nations of the new generation. The Women’s Olympiad promises an equally compelling competition. India will do their best to defend their 2024 title but a deep field of ambitious emerging federations have travelled far and wide to challenge them. Both the Open line-up and the Women’s line-up were discussed in detail in our previous sports preview a few weeks ago. Winning an Olympiad is a test of consistency as much as strength. Over 11 rounds, every team will face moments when it is expected to win, moments when it must defend, and inevitably a few matches where everything is at stake. The challenge is to keep the four players performing together day after day. As in relay teams or rowing crews, one exceptional performer cannot compensate indefinitely for weaknesses elsewhere. Captains must constantly judge in their pre-match strategy when to push for victory and when a solid result is the best practical choice. In an event this long and competitive, maintaining the right balance throughout the two weeks can be as important as playing the strongest chess.There is no single road to the podium: each team will create its own tournament as the rounds unfold. And yet the 46th Olympiad is about much more than the two main events.For the next two weeks, Samarkand will become the capital of world chess.The 3rd FIDE Chess Olympiad for People with Disabilities is currently in full swing, bringing together a record 41 teams representing players with visual, hearing and physical impairments. And off the board, the FIDE Congress and elections will take place, during which the international chess community will discuss the future direction of the sport. One of the key commissions will be the FIDE Summit on Chess in Education, scheduled for September 24, congregating educators, policymakers and researchers together as part of FIDE’s 2026 Year of Chess in Education. On a more technical note, the important meeting for team captains will be held at the Tashkent Ball room in the Hilton Samarkand Regency hotel at 3 PM on September 15. Meanwhile, the traditional torch relay ceremony was performed today in India. FIDE Interim President GM Vishy Anand and Mr. Nitin Narang, President of the All India Chess Federation, handed the torch with the Olympic flame over to GM Javokhir Sindarov, who will travel with it to the Samarkand Olympiad. Official website: https://chessolympiad2026.fide.com/ Written by Michael Rahal Photos: Stev Bonhage, Mark Livshitz and Lennart Ootes
